teaser.en: Its ribbon leaves can grow a metre long, streaming in the tide like green tape in the shallow lagoons.

summary.en: Tape seagrass is the largest seagrass on the coast, with long ribbon leaves up to a metre long, and one of the predominant seagrasses in Kenya. Its meadows in sheltered lagoons are nurseries for the fish that Digo fishers catch.

about.en:
Tape seagrass is a flowering plant that lives fully submerged in the sea. It is the giant among seagrasses: its long, flat ribbon leaves can reach a metre in length, rising from a thick, creeping stem covered in tough black fibres from old leaves.

At low tide the leaves lie flat on the water's surface. Its pollination is unusual: tiny male flowers break free and float on the surface to reach the female flowers.

where.en: It grows in shallow, sheltered lagoons with muddy sand and is one of the predominant seagrasses in Kenya. Seagrass meadows fringe Gazi Bay, Diani-Chale and Vanga-Shimoni. Look for its long ribbons lying on the surface of the lagoon at low tide.

uses.en: Its meadows are habitat for the rabbitfish, parrotfish, octopus and sea cucumbers that Digo fishers depend on. They also trap sediment and help to protect beaches.

names.en: No Digo name has been recorded yet. Swahili speakers usually call sea plants in general *mwani*. In English it is tape seagrass, and its scientific name is *Enhalus acoroides*.

conservation.en: The seagrass meadows of Gazi Bay, Diani-Chale and Vanga-Shimoni are feeding grounds for dugongs, green turtles and rabbitfish, and nurseries for young fish.

reason.en: Farmed in the same shallow lagoons
